strengths: Principled theoretical foundation: Theorem 1 establishes rigorous sufficient conditions under which replacing the standard terminal Gaussian prior with an estimated conditional Gaussian distribution reduces the KL divergence to the data distribution. The training objective for the Joint Mean-Covariance Estimator (JMCE) is directly derived from these theoretical bounds.

Unified and modular framework: CW-Gen generalizes earlier prior-informed generative frameworks (such as CARD/TMDM using mean priors and NsDiff using diagonal variance) to full inter-variable conditional covariance. It seamlessly plugs into multiple diffusion backbones (CW-Diff) as well as flow matching models (CW-Flow).

Comprehensive empirical validation: The method is evaluated across five benchmark datasets and integrated with six state-of-the-art generative models. The evaluation covers both probabilistic (CRPS, QICE, ProbCorr, Conditional FID) and point forecasting metrics over 10 independent random seeds with reported standard deviations.

Extensive ablations and practical efficiency analyses: The paper provides in-depth ablations on the regularizer, eigenvalue threshold, backbone architectures, sliding window lengths, and demonstrates practical acceleration techniques (such as lower-triangular inversion replacing full eigen-decomposition) as well as end-to-end training.
weaknesses: Scalability bottlenecks in high dimensions: Estimating and regularizing full $d \times d$ sliding-window covariance matrices incurs $O(d^3 T_f)$ computational complexity during SVD and Cholesky/eigen-decomposition. As shown in Table 19 for Solar Energy ($d=137$), training time increases substantially compared to low-dimensional datasets. Further exploration of structured low-rank or sparse covariance parameterizations for very large $d$ would strengthen the approach.

Block-diagonal temporal assumption in the prior: The conditional covariance is parameterized per time step $t \in \{1, \dots, T_f\}$ with shape $d \times d \times T_f$, effectively assuming temporal block-independence in the base prior noise, leaving cross-temporal correlations entirely to the backbone score/velocity network.

strengths: Principled theoretical foundation: The proposed framework derives sufficient conditions (Theorem 1) under which replacing the standard Gaussian prior with an estimated conditional Gaussian reduces the KL divergence to the target distribution. The derivation cleanly informs the design of the training objective in JMCE, including the Frobenius norm, nuclear norm, and eigenvalue penalty terms.

Methodological generality and simplicity: Conditionally Whitening (CW) transforms the data into a near-stationary, decorrelated space before applying generative modeling. This decouples prior modeling from the generative reverse process, avoiding complex heuristic modifications during sampling (such as those required by NsDiff) and allowing plug-and-play integration with DDPM, bridge models, and Flow Matching.

Thorough and comprehensive evaluation: The empirical evaluation benchmarks six diverse generative models (TimeDiff, SSSD, Diffusion-TS, TMDM, NsDiff, FlowTS) across five real-world datasets spanning different domains, resolutions, and dimensions, with 10 random seeds per experiment.

Strong empirical gains across diverse metrics: CW-Gen demonstrates solid improvements across predictive accuracy (CRPS, QICE), point forecasts (ProbMSE, ProbMAE), multi-variable dependency modeling (ProbCorr), and distribution distance (Conditional FID).

Extensive ablations and practical extensions: The appendix provides extensive ablations examining hyperparameters, architectural backbones, component contributions (mean only vs. variance only vs. full covariance), sliding window lengths, computational complexity mitigations (via triangular Cholesky substitution), and end-to-end training.
weaknesses: Computational scalability on high-dimensional data: Predicting and regularizing a $d \times d$ sliding-window covariance at every forecast step $t \in \{1, \dots, T_f\}$ incurs non-trivial computational overhead. As reported in Table 19, on the 137-dimensional Solar dataset, JMCE training and conditional whitening require significantly more compute than baseline methods, primarily due to eigenvalue decompositions and SVDs during training.

Gap between sliding-window covariance and true conditional covariance: The theoretical results assume access to the true conditional covariance $\Sigma_{X|C}$, whereas in practice JMCE optimizes against a temporal sliding-window sample covariance proxy $\tilde{\Sigma}_{X_0, t}$. While practically justified, the theoretical consequences of this approximation deserve more explicit discussion.

Main body readability and deferred content: A substantial amount of critical analysis, full benchmark tables for 4 out of 5 datasets, and algorithm descriptions are deferred to the supplementary material, making the main text somewhat dense and reliant on the appendix for full context.

strengths: Clear motivation: Standard conditional diffusion and flow matching models often rely on an uninformative standard Gaussian prior, while existing prior-informed models (e.g., CARD, TMDM, NsDiff) either only regress the conditional mean or ignore inter-variable cross-covariances. Conditionally whitening both mean and full inter-variable covariance is a natural, principled framework.

Theoretically motivated objective: Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 establish sufficient conditions under which replacing the standard terminal prior with an estimated Gaussian prior reduces the KL divergence to the true conditional distribution. This directly motivates the loss formulation in JMCE, particularly the eigenvalue barrier/penalty that prevents the factor from blowing up.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The authors validate the framework across six diverse generative models (TimeDiff, SSSD, Diffusion-TS, TMDM, NsDiff, FlowTS) on five benchmark datasets, evaluating both probabilistic metrics (CRPS, QICE, ProbCorr, Conditional FID) and point metrics (ProbMSE, ProbMAE). The framework consistently improves baseline performance in the vast majority of settings.

Extensive analysis and ablation studies: The paper provides in-depth investigations into hyperparameter sensitivity (e.g., eigenvalue penalty weight, sliding window length), backbone architectures, individual prior components (mean vs. variance vs. full covariance), and an end-to-end training variant.
weaknesses: Theoretical disconnect between target and estimation: Theorem 1 assumes convergence towards the true conditional covariance $\Sigma_{X|C}$. However, in practice, the model is trained against the empirical sliding-window covariance $\tilde{\Sigma}_{X_0, t}$ computed from a single realization/trajectory. The gap between the empirical sliding-window covariance of a single sequence and the true conditional covariance across the data-generating process is not formally bounded or analyzed.

Scalability to high-dimensional time series: Estimating a full $d \times d$ lower-triangular matrix for every forecast time step $t \in \{1, \dots, T_f\}$ requires predicting $T_f \cdot d(d+1)/2$ entries and running matrix operations (eigen-decomposition, SVD, matrix inversion). As shown in Table 19 for Solar Energy ($d=137$), training time scales significantly, which limits practical applicability to high-dimensional problems (e.g., large sensor networks or traffic datasets where $d > 500$).

Incomplete analysis of the total reverse diffusion error: Theorem 1 strictly analyzes the KL divergence between the true distribution and the terminal Gaussian distribution $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{X|C} \parallel \hat{Q})$. While a closer terminal distribution reduces one component of the forward/reverse error, the paper does not theoretically quantify how conditional whitening impacts the score estimation error or discretization error along the reverse trajectory.

Inconsistent gains on certain prior-augmented baselines: On some datasets and baselines that already incorporate priors (e.g., NsDiff on ETTh1 in Table 2, where raw NsDiff achieves a CRPS of 0.407 vs. 0.431 for CW-NsDiff, and point forecasting on Solar Energy in Table 7), the benefits of CW-Gen are marginal or slightly degraded.

strengths: Principled theoretical motivation: The paper establishes a concrete sufficient condition (Theorem 1) under which modifying the terminal prior distribution of diffusion/flow matching models reduces the KL divergence to the data distribution, thereby guiding the loss function design.

Well-designed estimation objective: The proposed Joint Mean-Covariance Estimator (JMCE) directly mirrors the theoretical bound derived in Theorem 1, incorporating Frobenius, nuclear norm, and minimal eigenvalue penalization to ensure stability and positive-definiteness.

Broad applicability and versatility: CW-Gen is formulated as a general framework that can be instantiated with both SDE-based diffusion models (CW-Diff) and ODE-based flow matching models (CW-Flow), functioning as an effective plug-in module for various existing architectures.

Comprehensive empirical validation across base models: The method is tested across six representative generative baselines (TimeDiff, SSSD, Diffusion-TS, TMDM, NsDiff, FlowTS) on five benchmarks, showing consistent gains across probabilistic metrics (CRPS, QICE, ProbCorr, Conditional FID).
weaknesses: Approximation gap in covariance modeling: The whitening is applied per time step across spatial dimensions $d$ using a sliding-window covariance $\widehat{\Sigma}_{X_0, t|C} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$, effectively ignoring cross-temporal covariance dependencies in the whitening operation itself. The implications of this block-diagonal/temporal independence simplification should be more explicitly discussed.

Computational overhead and scalability: In CW-Diff, matrix square-root and inversion operations via eigen-decomposition scale as $\mathcal{O}(d^3 T_f)$. While CW-Flow mitigates this at sampling time, computing and backpropagating through SVD / eigenvalue constraints during JMCE training for high-dimensional datasets (e.g., Solar Energy with $d=137$) remains non-trivial. The paper lacks detailed reporting on training time, inference latency, and memory footprint comparisons against raw baselines.

Presentation of main empirical results: The main text only displays the detailed metric breakdown for ETTh1 (Table 2), relegating Tables 3–6 to the appendix. Providing a more consolidated table in the main body summarizing key probabilistic metrics across all five datasets would make the empirical claims significantly more self-contained.

strengths: Principled motivation and theoretical grounding: Theorem 1 establishes an explicit sufficient condition under which replacing the standard Gaussian prior with an estimated conditional Gaussian prior reduces the terminal KL divergence, providing a clear mathematical justification for prior-informed generative modeling.

Unified and elegant framework: The proposed Conditional Whitening (CW) simplifies and unifies prior incorporation across generative paradigms—formulated as data standardization for diffusion models (CW-Diff) and as base distribution reparameterization for flow matching (CW-Flow), avoiding the overly complicated reverse processes seen in prior works such as NsDiff.

Well-designed joint estimator (JMCE): Guided by Theorem 1, JMCE utilizes Cholesky decomposition to guarantee positive definiteness and introduces eigenvalue regularization to prevent rank deficiency and numerical instability.

Broad baseline compatibility: CW-Gen is model-agnostic and demonstrated to enhance a wide variety of existing architectures, including both prior-free and prior-informed diffusion and flow matching baselines.
weaknesses: Incomplete empirical reporting in the main paper: While Table 1 lists overall win rates and Table 2 reports full results on ETTh1, the text repeatedly references Tables 3–6 and Tables 7–8 for the remaining four datasets (ETTh2, ILI, Weather, Solar Energy) and additional metrics, but these tables are missing from the main body and relegated to an omitted appendix.

Scalability and computational complexity for high dimensions: Estimating a $d \times d$ sliding-window covariance at every forecast step $t \in \{1, \dots, T_f\}$ requires predicting $T_f \times d(d+1)/2$ elements. For high-dimensional datasets such as Solar Energy ($d=137, T_f=192$), this represents a substantial parameter and memory overhead. Moreover, CW-Diff requires $T_f$ matrix eigen-decompositions ($O(d^3 T_f)$); the main text lacks empirical runtime and memory benchmarks comparing CW models against the raw baselines.

Temporal cross-covariance is ignored: The whitening transformation operates block-wise across time ($d \times d$ for each time step $t$), capturing instantaneous cross-variable correlations but omitting cross-time covariances ($d T_f \times d T_f$). The assumptions and limitations behind this temporal independence simplification should be more explicitly discussed.

Practical verifiability of Theorem 1: The sufficient condition in Eq. (3) includes the dimensional scaling factor $\sqrt{d_x} \|\Sigma_{X|C} - \hat{\Sigma}_{X|C}\|_F$. In high dimensions, satisfying this inequality requires very low estimation error. An empirical verification demonstrating whether and how often condition (3) holds on real datasets would significantly strengthen the theoretical narrative.

strengths: Clear conceptual motivation: The paper addresses key challenges in multivariate probabilistic time series forecasting—such as non-stationarity, heteroscedasticity, and inter-feature dependencies—by proposing a unified conditional whitening framework (CW-Gen) applicable to both diffusion models (CW-Diff) and flow matching (CW-Flow).

Theoretical guidance for loss design: Theorem 1 provides sufficient conditions under which replacing the standard normal terminal distribution with an estimated conditional Gaussian reduces KL divergence, which directly motivates the loss formulation (including eigenvalue regularization) of the Joint Mean-Covariance Estimator (JMCE).

Broad experimental coverage across baselines: The framework is evaluated across six diverse generative models (TimeDiff, SSSD, Diffusion-TS, TMDM, NsDiff, FlowTS) and five benchmark datasets, showing widespread empirical gains across multiple probabilistic evaluation metrics (CRPS, QICE, ProbCorr, Conditional FID).
weaknesses: Incremental methodological novelty: At its core, CW-Diff acts as a learned two-stage normalization/whitening preprocessing step ($X^{CW} = \hat{\Sigma}^{-1/2}(X - \hat{\mu})$) followed by standard generative modeling on residuals. While extending mean/marginal variance adjustment (as in TMDM and NsDiff) to sliding-window covariance is natural, the conceptual advance over prior residual/prior-informed generative models is modest.

Neglect of temporal cross-covariances in whitening: The whitening transformation is applied purely across spatial/feature dimensions at each time step $t$ using sliding-window covariance $\hat{\Sigma}_{X_0,t|C} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$, rather than modeling full spatiotemporal covariance across $d \times T_f$. The implications, limitations, and potential boundary artifacts of using local sliding-window approximations warrant deeper theoretical and empirical justification.

Computational overhead and scalability: For CW-Diff, matrix square-root and inversion via eigen-decomposition requires $O(d^3 T_f)$ operations per sample/step. On higher-dimensional datasets (e.g., Solar Energy with $d=137$), this introduces noticeable computational cost during both training and inference. The paper lacks detailed profiling of training time, inference latency, and memory footprint compared to baseline models.

Presentation and reporting of main empirical results: The main paper provides detailed performance numbers only for ETTh1 (Table 2), relegating the full performance tables of the remaining four datasets (ETTh2, ILI, Weather, Solar Energy) to the appendix and summarizing them only via aggregated 'win rates' in Table 1.
